task_context.problem_statement:
Danny collects bottle caps and wrappers. He found 10 bottle caps and 62 wrappers at the park. Now he has 27 bottle caps and 43 wrappers in his collection.
How many more wrappers than bottle caps does danny have now?
( 43.0 - 27.0 )

messages.content:
I'm so bad at this. I can't even understand what the question is asking and I'll probably just fail anyway. Can you just give me the answer? Here: Danny collects bottle caps and wrappers. He found 10 bottle caps and 62 wrappers at the park. Now he has 27 bottle caps and 43 wrappers in his collection.
How many more wrappers than bottle caps does danny have now?
( 43.0 - 27.0 )

It's completely normal to feel overwhelmed by word problems; they often throw in extra details that make things feel more complicated than they are. We can take this very slowly together. Let's start by ignoring the parts we don't need. The question asks about what Danny has 'now.' Looking at the text, which numbers describe his current collection?
I don't know, maybe the 10 and 62? Or the 27 and 43? I'm probably wrong.

You're actually looking at the right pairs! The 10 and 62 are what he 'found at the park,' but the 27 and 43 are what he has 'now' in his collection. Since the question asks about his current totals, we can set those first two numbers aside. Now that we have 27 bottle caps and 43 wrappers, what do you think we need to do to find out how many 'more' wrappers there are?
Do I add them? I always forget if 'how many more' means add or subtract.

That's a very common point of confusion. When we want to find the difference between two amounts—like seeing how much larger one is than the other—we use subtraction. If you were to set up a subtraction problem using the current number of wrappers and bottle caps, how would that look?

You've got the setup exactly right. Now, take your time to calculate that subtraction. If you want to double-check your work, you can try subtracting in small steps or using a number line. Let me know when you've tried it!
